opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest advantage is focus. OpenAI and DeepMind are extraordinary organizations, but they are fighting on many fronts at once: consumer products, enterprise, coding, multimodal, safety, policy. Mathematics, or formal reasoning more specifically, is one important line item among dozens for them. For us, it is the whole company. Every hire, every compute dollar, every architectural decision points at one question: how do we build an AI that can actually do rigorous mathematics and prove that what it says is correct?

That focus compounds. When you only care about one problem, you can make bets that wouldn't survive a big lab's internal prioritization. For example, we're betting heavily on formal verification, on languages like Lean, where every step of a proof is checked by a machine. For a general-purpose lab, that can look like a niche: the data is scarce, the tooling is immature, and it doesn't immediately show up in a chatbot product. For us, that is the point. Verified reasoning gives you a ground-truth signal, and that's incredibly valuable for training, for reinforcement learning, and eventually for trust.

The second advantage is talent density and the kind of people you can attract. There's a specific type of person who sits at the intersection of serious mathematics and serious machine learning: people who have done olympiad math or a math PhD and also know how to train models. There aren't many of them. Many of them would rather be at a place where their work is the core mission, not a side project. A startup can offer them ownership: you're not one of three thousand researchers, you are the person building the prover.

Third is speed. We don't have layers of review or product committees. If we see something in the morning that suggests an approach is wrong, we can change direction by the afternoon. In a field that moves this fast, iteration speed matters as much as raw resources.

I don't want to be naive about it, though. Compute is a real asymmetry, and we can't out-scale them on general pretraining. So the strategy isn't to beat them at their own game. It's to pick a game where depth, data quality, and verification matter more than sheer scale, and to go deeper than anyone else is willing to. If we do that well, we may end up with things that matter to the big labs too: verified reasoning data, formal libraries, provers. That's a good position for a small team.

r001.rationale: The response describes focus, talent density, and faster iteration as startup advantages, but it does not state that startups need fewer resources per unit of innovation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you don't win by doing what they do, just smaller. If you try to out-scale OpenAI or DeepMind on general language models, you'll lose. They have more compute, more data, more people, and more distribution. So the advantage has to come from somewhere structural, not from working harder.

For us at Axiom, the structural advantage is focus. We care about one thing: can a machine actually do mathematics, not just talk about it. The big labs are optimizing for a product that serves hundreds of millions of people, and math is one line item among many. For us it's the whole company. That means every research decision, every hire, every dataset we build is pointed at a single problem. You'd be surprised how much that compounds. A small team that thinks about formal reasoning every single day will notice things a general team simply doesn't have time to notice.

The second thing is that in a domain like mathematics, the bottleneck isn't raw scale, it's verification and the right training signal. If you have a formal system like Lean, you don't need a human to tell you whether an answer is right. The proof either checks or it doesn't. That shifts the game from "who has more human-labeled data" to "who designs the better loop between generation and verification." That's a research question, and research questions can be won by a small group with good taste.

Third, speed and risk tolerance. A large lab has to justify things to a roadmap, to safety reviews, to product teams. We can decide on Monday to throw out an approach and try something else by Wednesday. We can also work on problems that look unpromising from the outside, where the payoff is uncertain and five years away. Big organizations are structurally bad at that kind of bet.

And finally, talent. The best mathematicians and the best ML researchers who care about mathematics are a very small group of people. Many of them don't want to be a cog in a thousand-person org. They want to work on the problem itself, with people who understand it. A startup can offer that in a way the big labs genuinely can't.

So I'd say: we're not competing with them on their terms. We're trying to be the place where a specific, very hard problem gets solved first. If we do that, the scale question answers itself later.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes focus, verification, speed, and talent as startup advantages, but does not state that startups require fewer resources per unit of innovation.

astra-6.text:
I think an early-stage startup’s advantage is focus and speed. You don’t have to compete with OpenAI or DeepMind on every dimension. You can pick a specific problem, get very close to the people who have it, and learn faster than a larger organization can.

The hard part is choosing a problem where that learning compounds—where you’re building something more valuable than a feature that disappears with the next model release. If better models make your product more useful, and you have a deep understanding of your customers’ workflow, then the big labs’ progress can actually work in your favor.

r001.rationale: The response highlights focus, speed, and faster customer learning, but does not state that startups require fewer resources per unit of innovation than OpenAI and DeepMind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an early-stage startup’s advantage is focus. You’re probably not going to outspend OpenAI or DeepMind, so you need to choose a specific problem where you can learn faster and execute really well.

A small team can work directly with users, make decisions quickly, and change direction without coordinating across a large organization. That matters especially when you’re still figuring out what people actually need. The opportunity is to find something the big labs aren’t prioritizing and build a tight feedback loop around it. Being small only helps if you turn that into speed and insight.

r001.rationale: The response says startups cannot outspend OpenAI or DeepMind and can move faster, but it does not state that they require fewer resources per unit of innovation.
